title: Local Kan planning and MCP integration are operational
content: The workspace now has a working local Kan planning service, a dedicated agent connection, and an imported Trello board. Reviewed workspace changes added the deployment, operational tooling, and documentation. This is development infrastructure for planning and coordination, not a product release or a public planning service. A deliberately local deployment Kan 0.7.0 and its matching migration image run as pinned containers alongside PostgreSQL 15.20. Migrations must finish before the application starts, and the database has no host-published port. Live state belongs to a Docker named volume that survives container replacement and an ordinary service shutdown. Only the browser-facing Kan listener is published, and it is bound to the local loopback interface. There is no Caddy service, domain name, public certificate, LAN binding, or inbound firewall change in this design. Creating the first owner uses a temporary loopback-only registration phase; normal operation requires unrestricted registration to remain disabled. The service is intentionally small. Email delivery, S3 uploads, Redis, OAuth, and hosted MCP are not configured. Kan’s public documentation covers the upstream application; the deployment deliberately limits its scope. Kan coordinates planned work, while GitHub repositories, pull requests, CI records, and human approvals remain the source of engineering truth. A card cannot prove that code was reviewed, merged, or released. Dedicated agent access through MCP The agent connection uses the pinned @kan.bn/mcp 0.1.0 package and a locked dependency tree. It runs over local stdio rather than opening another network service. A wrapper retrieves the dedicated account’s API token from the user’s Secret Service when the process starts; the token is not stored in the Kilo configuration, repository files, chat, or command-line arguments. The agent is a separate non-admin member of the Kan workspace, not the human owner. Workspace membership and regular-board membership are separate: the latest live check found one accessible board, and additional boards require explicit assignment. Kilo permits ordinary reads, asks before ordinary writes, and denies deletion, invitations, member-role changes, and workspace administration. Those client-side rules supplement rather than replace Kan’s own permissions. The MCP handshake registered 46 tools. Authenticated workspace, member-role, workspace-detail, and board-list reads passed, as did an unknown-workspace negative check. This does not mean every tool was exercised. The upstream list_members operation returned 404 against this Kan version, so verification uses get_workspace instead. A new verification option also fails when required board access is absent rather than treating an empty list as success. Importing and checking real work Static checks, real-image behavioral smoke tests, and a two-version backup and recovery rehearsal passed. They covered registration gating, invitations, board objects, persistence, archive validation, restored board/card/checklist content, and preservation of the original database during a failed restore. The operator then completed a Trello import successfully. The importer creates new boards rather than maintaining continuous synchronization, and repeating an import creates duplicates. In this Kan version, comments, attachments, members, archived items, and due dates are not imported; unnamed labels are dropped and exact card ordering is not guaranteed. The successful import is an operator acceptance result, not an independent field-by-field audit. Backups and remaining operational work Real online PostgreSQL backups were taken before and after the import. Both passed dump-readability, image-provenance, and checksum verification. Kan and ntfy now have separate product directories in the shared backup hierarchy, and the earlier ntfy archive was copied into it without changing its contents or deleting the original. Those archives are protected local copies on the same filesystem, not off-host backups. They have not been restored into an isolated staging stack, and no external-disk export, recurring schedule, retention routine, or external health monitor is configured yet. Those steps remain necessary before relying on this as a complete recovery and retention practice. The live Kan version is pinned. Isolated recovery tests do not provide a live upgrade or rollback procedure, so those operations remain blocked until a separately reviewed executable runbook exists. The MCP dependency audit also reports a known high-severity availability advisory with no compatible fix; a 512 MiB process heap limit is only a partial mitigation, not a claim that the integration is vulnerability-free. For ordinary browser-based planning, the integration is usable now. For agent use, board membership remains deliberate and limited. The remaining work is operational hardening: protected off-host recovery evidence, monitoring, token maintenance, and a safe upgrade path—not another claim that a merged change is a released product.

title: LAN-only ntfy deployment is operational
content: The workspace now has a working ntfy notification service on its trusted development LAN. A reviewed workspace change added the deployment, its operational tooling, and shared backup helpers. The public infrastructure policy describes the service’s role and ownership boundaries. This is development infrastructure, not a product release or a notification integration for any Heretical application. What is in place The deployment uses the upstream ntfy 2.38.0 container, selected by an exact version and immutable image digest. A single Docker Compose service keeps its account database and a 12-hour message cache outside Git. The container runs without root privileges, has a read-only root filesystem, drops capabilities except for binding its HTTP listener, and has bounded logs and explicit resource limits. Network access is deliberately narrower than a normal hosted ntfy installation. The service binds to one configured private LAN address and uses direct HTTP, with no public DNS, Internet forwarding, reverse proxy, or TLS endpoint. Host firewall rules allow that port only through the selected trusted interface and approved local source prefixes. A dedicated firewall chain is installed before service startup and removed after shutdown; other Docker and host rules are left alone. This design is suitable only for the controlled LAN and does not provide transport encryption or off-LAN access. Authentication still matters on that LAN. Anonymous access is denied, and separate publisher and consumer identities have scoped permissions. Each device or producer receives its own labeled, expiring token rather than sharing an administrator credential. The operator guide covers topic naming, account grants, token rotation, Android enrollment, and desktop subscriptions without recording live credentials in the repository. Verification so far The implementation passed 155 static and mocked lifecycle checks, 43 isolated behavioral smoke checks, and 55 synthetic backup, restore, upgrade, and rollback checks. These cover configuration rendering, address restrictions, firewall ordering and rollback, positive and negative ACL cases, HTTP and WebSocket streaming, persistence, and recovery safeguards. The operator then deployed the pinned container and confirmed its health, actual LAN filtering, scoped account behavior, Android access, and manual HTTP streaming. A real cold backup completed successfully, its SHA-256 sidecar verified, and the service returned to a healthy state. Those observations are recorded as a single-host deployment result, not as proof of high availability or guaranteed delivery. Android accepts the server when its complete http:// URL is supplied. Plain-HTTP delivery can still be limited to opening or refreshing the application, so the current setup does not promise instant background push on mobile devices. The supplied Android capture shows the test messages arriving in the application. It is a client-delivery observation, not a claim about delivery when the server or LAN is unavailable. Backups and remaining work The new shared backup registry records non-secret, machine-local paths and gives each product its own archive and disk-export namespace. ntfy owns safe archive creation; shared helpers only discover, copy, and verify completed archives and checksum sidecars. A disk export must be on an explicitly mounted, separate filesystem, preventing a second directory on the same host disk from being mistaken for off-host protection. The first production archive has not yet been restored into an isolated staging container or copied to an external disk. Recurring backup scheduling, retention, and LAN health monitoring are also still operator tasks. Those are the next acceptance steps before treating the service as having a tested recovery and retention routine. No Kan, Woodpecker, or product-specific notification client was added. Notifications remain non-authoritative signals; repositories, reviews, CI records, and human approvals remain the source of engineering decisions.

title: Doxygen documentation portal is live
content: The Heretical Documentation portal is now live. It brings selected workspace and product documentation together without moving that material out of its owning repositories. This is deployed development infrastructure, not a product release: no engine, framework, editor, or library release is implied. What was built The portal has its own source repository, Heretical-Solutions/Heretical-Documentation, and builds with Doxygen 1.18.0 and Doxygen Awesome CSS 2.5.0. Both the generator release and theme revision are pinned and verified. Doxygen is restored for the build rather than installed globally or committed as a binary; the theme is restored from a locked Git commit. Authoritative eng/ commands cover restore, build, local preview, and validation. The build aggregates explicitly selected Markdown documents into ignored intermediates, preserves relative links and media, and records source provenance. Canonical documentation stays in its original repository. The current publication includes workspace architecture, policies, repository records, and the blog’s product guides. It does not invent API sections for products that publish no library API. Source and integration A reviewed workspace change registered the portal as an independent submodule. The initial publication used pinned source revisions for the private workspace input and public website sources: Input Revision Private workspace documentation Reviewed source snapshot; exact revision retained in the internal build record Portal master e02da8b27803a4c172a6928bf13976241bdf9c8e Blog master 1c505359e5b4afb9323906b4b4589b00e676f57f The generated source provenance page records the inputs for the published site. Source aggregation, portal registration, and website deployment remain separate operations with separate review gates. Validation and publication The portal passed local validation, a clean canonical recursive checkout, and its GitHub Actions build. Checks covered source and tool pins, internal links and fragments, document coverage, navigation assets, payload hygiene, and the project Pages base path. A separate C# extraction fixture passed without Unity, .asmdef resolution, generated project files, compilation, or stubs. That fixture demonstrates source extraction only; it does not prove Unity compatibility, compilation, or runtime behavior. Final workflow run #3 restored the selected inputs, validated the site, uploaded the Pages artifact, and deployed it successfully. The live catalog, blog guides, search resources, and required license texts were checked, and desktop and mobile Firefox renders were inspected. The mobile layout collapses the documentation tree behind a navigation control while keeping search and the light/dark control available. Boundaries and remaining checks The portal deploys through its own GitHub Actions workflow to GitHub project Pages. The blog keeps its separate repository, manual editorial process, and gh-pages publication history. Neither site uses a custom domain in this phase. Because the canonical superproject is private, full CI source restore uses a narrowly scoped read-only credential; untrusted pull requests receive no source credential and run structural checks only. The initial supported build host is Linux x86_64. No versioned documentation, product API reference, or release compatibility claim has been added. Interactive search, theme-toggle, and browser-console review remain manual acceptance checks. Future product sections will come from real registered repositories and their own canonical documentation.

title: Blog repository initialised
content: The development blog now exists as its own first-party repository, Heretical-Solutions/Heretical-Blog, with its source checked out in the workspace at sites/blog/. Superproject registration is a separate later step. This post records what was set up; it makes no claim about any product being released. What is in place A Jekyll site using the Chirpy theme consumed as a packaged gem, pinned by a committed Gemfile.lock. Site identity, UTC dates, search, categories, tags, Atom feed, syntax highlighting, and responsive light/dark mode. Comments, analytics, and PWA/offline caching are disabled. Authoritative commands under eng/ for dependency restore, a local preview server, a production build into the ignored artifacts/site/ directory, and validation. Product documentation for requirements, build, quick start, editorial process, deployment, and compatibility. Publication model for now Publication is deliberately manual. Approved source is committed to master, built and validated locally, then published as a deployment-only gh-pages branch for GitHub project Pages at /Heretical-Blog/. Generated HTML never lands on master, and each deployment commit records the source revision it came from. Superproject registration is reviewed separately from product publication. There are no GitHub Actions workflows, repository webhooks, or automatic draft generation in this initial phase. Build/deploy automation and event-driven editorial drafts are separate later proposals, each with its own approval gate. Editorial process _drafts/ is the single draft queue. A human reviewer promotes approved content into _posts/, and production builds exclude drafts, so unreviewed material cannot reach the published site.
